opus-5.5.text:
I think the recurring waves come from a tension that never really goes away. Softmax attention is wonderful for quality, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length during training, and at inference the KV cache keeps growing with every token you generate. So whenever the field pushes toward longer contexts, whether that's long documents, agents running many steps, or reasoning models producing very long chains of thought, people start asking again whether there's a cheaper way. Linear attention is the obvious candidate, because it compresses the whole history into a fixed-size state, so you get constant memory and linear compute.

The first wave, around 2020, was mostly about the math. Katharopoulos and colleagues showed that if you drop the softmax and use a kernel feature map, attention can be rewritten as an RNN. It was elegant, but the quality gap on language modeling was significant, and on the hardware side it often wasn't faster in practice. Interest faded.

The next wave came with state space models and then Mamba, and also RetNet and GLA, which my collaborators and I worked on. Two things changed. One was gating, or data-dependent decay: letting the model decide how much of its memory to forget at each step turned out to matter a lot for quality. The other was hardware-efficient algorithms. Naive linear attention is a recurrence, which isn't friendly to GPUs. With chunkwise parallel forms you can use matrix multiplications inside chunks and only do the recurrence across chunks, so it actually runs fast on tensor cores. That's what made people take it seriously again.

After that, the focus moved to how the state gets updated. With DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, instead of just adding new key-value associations to memory, you use the delta rule: you first check what the memory currently returns for a key and then correct the error. That's closer to online learning, a test-time-training view, and it substantially improves retrieval and in-context recall, which was the known weakness of these models. We also worked out how to parallelize the delta rule efficiently, which was the key to scaling it.

And now I think we're in a more practical wave, where the question isn't "can linear attention replace softmax attention" but "how do we combine them." Hybrid models that mix a few full-attention layers with many linear or delta-rule layers keep most of the quality while greatly reducing KV cache and inference cost. Several industry models have gone in this direction, which gives the area much more legitimacy than when it was mostly academic.

So I'd say each wave follows the same pattern: a real need for efficiency, a new idea that narrows the quality gap, and an algorithm that makes it fast on actual hardware. When all three line up, interest returns. When one is missing, it fades. I don't expect pure linear attention to replace everything, but the fixed-size-memory idea is too valuable to disappear, especially as contexts and reasoning traces keep getting longer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the waves track the pain points of the dominant architecture at each moment, and they recede whenever hardware or engineering finds a cheaper fix than changing the architecture.

The first wave, around 2020, came from the quadratic cost of softmax attention. Papers like Linear Transformer and Performer showed that if you replace the softmax kernel with a feature map, attention becomes a recurrence with a constant-size state. That was elegant, but the quality gap was large and nobody had a training recipe that was actually faster on GPUs. Then FlashAttention arrived and made quadratic attention fast enough that most people stopped caring. The theoretical complexity argument lost to a good kernel.

The second wave came from state space models, S4 and then Mamba. The framing changed from "approximate attention" to "build a good recurrent model from first principles." Mamba's selectivity mechanism, which is really data-dependent gating, closed much of the quality gap at small scale. And people realized that gated linear attention, Mamba, RWKV, RetNet are all the same family: a linear recurrence over a matrix-valued state with some decay. That unification is what drew me in, because once you see it as one family you can study the design space systematically instead of treating each paper as a separate invention.

The current wave is driven by inference economics rather than training cost. Long-context serving is dominated by KV cache memory, and reasoning models that generate tens of thousands of tokens make this worse. A constant-size state is suddenly very attractive. At the same time, the delta rule and test-time-training view gave us recurrences that are actually expressive, not just cheap, and hardware-efficient chunked algorithms let us train them at scale. That is why you see hybrid models from serious labs now, mixing a few full attention layers with mostly linear layers.

So my honest summary is that linear attention keeps coming back because the underlying problem never went away. Each time it fades it is because engineering patched the symptom. Each time it returns it is because the symptom got worse at a new scale, and the recurrent side got better in the meantime. I do not think the current wave fully replaces attention. I think the stable endpoint is hybrid, and the interesting research question is how little full attention you really need.

r001.rationale: The response identifies softmax attention’s quadratic cost as a recurring problem and connects the current wave to long-context serving. That communicates the context-scaling bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It mentions quadratic cost but does not explain that materializing the attention matrix in global memory caused substantial memory-transfer overhead.

r003.rationale: It says FlashAttention made quadratic attention fast enough that most people stopped seeking approximations, reducing the motivation for linear attention.

r004.rationale: It attributes the current wave to inference economics, including long-context serving and reasoning models generating tens of thousands of tokens.

r005.rationale: It says early linear attention lacked a training recipe that was faster on GPUs and credits hardware-efficient chunked algorithms with enabling training at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the interest comes in waves because the bottleneck keeps changing. The basic motivation is always attractive: standard attention becomes expensive as the sequence gets longer, so can we avoid constructing that full attention matrix?

But efficiency alone isn’t enough. You can make attention cheaper and then discover that you’ve lost something important in quality. Linear attention compresses the history into a fixed-size state, which is useful for efficient inference, but it also makes retaining and retrieving precise information more difficult. So people get excited about the efficiency, encounter the quality gap, and the excitement cools down.

Then something changes—longer contexts become useful, a better architecture appears, or an implementation finally runs efficiently on the hardware—and people revisit the tradeoff. A theoretically efficient method isn’t necessarily fast in practice; the hardware implementation matters a lot.

So I don’t see these as simply repeated hype cycles. Each wave asks a slightly different question: can we make it work, can we make it competitive, and can we make its advantages matter in a real system?

r002.rationale: It mentions constructing the full attention matrix, but does not describe global-memory materialization, memory-transfer overhead, or the timing before Flash Attention.

r003.rationale: Flash Attention and its effect on the motivation to approximate softmax attention are not discussed.

r004.rationale: The response mentions efficient inference and useful longer contexts, but does not attribute a recent resurgence specifically to the cost of long-text decoding.

r005.rationale: It says theoretical efficiency does not guarantee practical speed, that the hardware implementation matters, and that advantages must matter in a real system, identifying hardware efficiency as necessary for practical acceptance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interest comes in waves because the promise is very compelling, but the tradeoffs keep changing. With standard attention, the cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention offers a way to avoid that, and during autoregressive decoding you can maintain a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache. So whenever people push toward longer contexts, the idea becomes attractive again.

The difficulty is that efficiency alone is not enough. You’re compressing the history into a state, and you have to preserve the information the model needs. A method can look very efficient on paper and still struggle with quality, especially when a task requires retrieving a specific detail from far back in the context.

And then there’s hardware efficiency. Linear complexity doesn’t automatically mean lower latency. Standard attention has very optimized implementations, so a linear attention model needs an algorithm that also maps well to the GPU.

So I see these waves as people revisiting the same fundamental opportunity with better architectures, better training recipes, and better kernels. The question each time is: can we retain more of attention’s capability while actually delivering the efficiency advantage?
